## Proof

The polylogarithm is defined by

$$\operatorname{Li}_s(z) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{z^n}{n^s}.$$

For $s=1$ this is the geometric-series-with-$1/n$-weight:

$$\operatorname{Li}_1(z) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{z^n}{n}.$$

This is a classical series whose closed form is obtained by integrating the geometric series termwise. Since

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} z^n = \frac{z}{1-z}, \qquad |z|<1,$$

integrating from $0$ to $z$ (valid for $|z|<1$) gives

$$\int_0^z \frac{t}{1-t}\,dt = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{z^n}{n} = \operatorname{Li}_1(z).$$

Computing the integral directly:

$$\int_0^z \frac{t}{1-t}\,dt = \int_0^z \left(\frac{1}{1-t}-1\right)dt = \bigl[-\ln(1-t)-t\bigr]_0^z = -\ln(1-z)-z.$$

Hence, exactly,

$$\operatorname{Li}_1(z) = -\ln(1-z), \qquad |z|<1.$$

Now take the limit $z\to 1^{-}$. Set $\varepsilon = 1-z$, so $\varepsilon \to 0^{+}$. Then

$$\operatorname{Li}_1(z) = -\ln(\varepsilon) = -\ln(1-z).$$

As $\varepsilon\to 0^+$, $-\ln\varepsilon \to +\infty$, and this logarithmic divergence dominates every bounded (or more slowly growing) correction. In particular, the next terms in any expansion around $z=1$ come from the analytic continuation structure of $\operatorname{Li}_s$ for $s\to 1$, where the well-known expansion

$$\operatorname{Li}_s(z) = \Gamma(1-s)(-\ln z)^{s-1} + \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \zeta(s-k)\frac{(\ln z)^k}{k!}$$

has the first term $\Gamma(1-s)(-\ln z)^{s-1}$, which diverges as $s\to 1$ since $\Gamma(1-s)\sim \frac{1}{1-s}-\gamma+\cdots$ and $(-\ln z)^{s-1}\to 1$. The divergence $\Gamma(1-s)\to\infty$ precisely produces the $-\ln(1-z)$ leading behavior, with the constant $\zeta(1)$ pole canceling against the $\Gamma$ pole to leave the finite logarithmic term. Thus the leading (dominant) asymptotic term is the logarithmic singularity

$$\operatorname{Li}_1(z) \sim -\ln(1-z), \qquad z\to 1^{-}.$$

All subleading contributions are $O(1)$ (constants such as $-z\to -1$, Euler–Mascheroni terms, etc.), so $-\ln(1-z)$ is unambiguously the leading term.

### PROOF COMPLETE
